EEG measures: ↑ left & right parietal theta and alpha, with sex differences.

Unexpected and highly unexpected chords triggered ERAN (amplitude ≈ varied with harmonic irregularity). Expression influenced N5 amplitude (↑ for expressive vs. unexpressive performance); ≈ P3a.
↑ frontal right alpha and beta (liked music). ↑ frontal‐midline theta for liked vs. disliked music.

EEG measures: ↑ High‐alpha power in left occipital region during last 50 s (full‐range vs. high‐cut music).

↑ Theta, low alpha‐1, low alpha‐2, upper alpha, and beta power (i.e., continuous ↑ event‐related synchronization). Positive correlations between acoustic variables (acoustic envelope, acoustic complexity) and power synchronization in each band.
ECG measures: ↓ HR in minute 2 (of 3 min listening). Negative correlation between acoustic complexity and HR.
EEG‐ECG interactions during music listen: Negative correlation between HR and the event‐related synchronization in each band across the time course of music listening.

EEG measures: ↓ Eigenvalues; slow song produced most significant decreases (T3, T4, P3). P3 most sensitive across all songs. T4 showed the greatest change in EEG dimensionality: most concentrated variance during slow song, most distributed during favorite song.

↑ coherence of EEG with cardiovascular and respiratory rhythms (see EEG‐ECG).
ECG measures: HR and IBI reported as part of coherence analysis (see EEG‐ECG).
EEG‐ECG interactions during music listen: ↑ coherence among cerebral, cardiovascular & respiratory rhythms during music listening. Slow tempo songs ↑ higher than fast; larger effect sizes in frontal region & right hemisphere.

ECG measures: ↑ HR (AVNN), proportional to pitch scaling. HRV measures modulated but α₁ (heart) not consistently affected.
EEG‐ECG interactions during music listen: Positive correlation between neuronal & cardiac dynamics during music listening.

ECG measures: IBI reported as part of coherence analysis (see EEG‐ECG).

EEG measures: EEG complexity ↑ with music complexity, showing strong correlation.
ECG measures: HRV complexity ↓ in response to music though not statistically significant.

EEG measures: Complexity of EEG ↑ with tempo & cognitive engagement, particularly for fast & favorite songs. Parietal & temporal lobes most affected; slow songs less complex; right hemisphere>left.

ECG measures: SE of HRV highest during rest; ↓ with each music presentation (inverse of EEG). HRV variations not significant.
EEG‐ECG interactions during music listen: Music, EEG & HRV SE changes correlated.
